pages.summary: A value shown with its name, as a statement without a semicolon shows it.
body: Called by the Command Window for every result left unsuppressed; a class can define its own `display` (or `disp`) to change how its objects show. `disp` shows the value without the name.

examples.title: Shown with and without the name

pages.summary: Input asked for in the Command Window, and a program stopped there to be looked at.
body: `input(prompt)` writes the prompt and waits for an answer, evaluated as an expression (`'s'` keeps it as text). `keyboard` stops the program at that point with the `K>>` prompt: variables can be looked at and changed, and `dbcont` goes on, `dbquit` stops. Both need someone at the Command Window, so they run in the page and not where these examples are run; the example writes a program that uses input, to run there.
syntax: Stop here until dbcont or dbquit.

examples.title: A program that asks until it gets a positive number

pages.summary: An error thrown: the program stops, unless a try block catches it.
body: The message may be a format with values (as `sprintf`); an identifier (`'component:mnemonic'`) before it lets a catch tell errors apart. `error(struct)` throws from a struct with fields `message` and `identifier`; an empty message throws nothing.

examples.title: Caught, with its identifier
examples.code:
try
    error('shape:badSide', 'A side of %g is not allowed.', -2);
catch e
    disp(e.identifier)
    disp(e.message)
end
examples.output:
shape:badSide
A side of -2 is not allowed.

pages.summary: Warnings shown, turned off and on, and the last warning and error.
body: `warning(msg)` writes the message and goes on. An identifier lets a warning be turned off (`warning('off', id)`) and on again; `warning('off', 'all')` turns all off. `lastwarn` gives the last warning's message and identifier, `lasterr` the last error's message.

examples.title: A warning shown, then silenced
examples.code:
warning('calc:slow', 'This may take %d seconds.', 5)
[msg, id] = lastwarn
warning('off', 'calc:slow')
warning('calc:slow', 'Not shown.')
warning('on', 'calc:slow')
examples.output:
Warning: This may take 5 seconds.
msg =

    'This may take 5 seconds.'

id =

    'calc:slow'

pages.summary: Exception objects: made, thrown, thrown again, given causes, and reported.
body: `MException(id, format, ...)` makes an exception without throwing it; `throw` throws it. A caught exception (`catch e`) can be thrown again with `rethrow`, keeping its stack, or `throwAsCaller` as if from the calling function. `addCause` attaches another exception as a cause; `getReport` gives the text the Command Window would show.

examples.title: An error with its cause
examples.output:
ans =

    'Could not read the record.'

ans =

    'Index exceeds the number of array elements. Index must not exceed 3.'

pages.summary: An error unless a condition holds.
body: For checks that should never fail: the error says the assertion failed, or gives the message (a format, with an identifier) when given.
syntax: With an identifier and formatted message.

examples.title: Checks that pass and one that does not
examples.code:
x = [1 2 3];
assert(all(x > 0))
try
    assert(numel(x) == 4, 'size:wrong', 'Expected 4 elements, got %d.', numel(x))
catch e
    disp(e.message)
end

pages.summary: An object that runs a function when it is cleared or goes out of scope.
body: Kept in a variable of a function, it runs its function when the function returns, whether normally or by an error: the way to close a file or restore a setting whatever happens.

examples.title: A setting restored when a function ends

pages.summary: Whether a name is a variable, a file, a built-in function or a folder.
body: 1 for a variable in the workspace, 2 for a file (a program file on the path or any file), 5 for a built-in function, 7 for a folder, and 0 when there is none; a second input asks about one kind only.

examples.title: Four kinds of name

pages.summary: Variables removed from the workspace (or functions, globals, everything).
body: `clear` alone removes all variables; names (with `*` wildcards) remove those; `clear -regexp` matches patterns; `clear global` the globals; `clear all` and `clear functions` also forget compiled functions. `clearvars -except` keeps some and removes the rest.

examples.title: Removing some, keeping some
examples.code:
a = 1; b = 2; temp1 = 3; temp2 = 4;
clear temp*
who
clearvars -except a
who
examples.output:
Your variables are:

a  b  


Your variables are:

a

pages.summary: The variables listed: by name, or with their sizes, bytes and classes.
body: Names (with `*` wildcards) list only those; `-file` lists the variables of a MAT-file. With an output, `who` gives a cell of names and `whos` a struct array with fields `name`, `size`, `bytes` and `class`.

examples.title: A few variables
examples.output:
Your variables are:

c  name  x  

  Name      Size            Bytes  Class     Attributes

  c         1x2               224  cell      
  name      1x4                 8  char      
  x         3x3                72  double    

ans =

    72

pages.summary: Text run as code; and run with what it writes captured.
body: `eval` runs a statement or evaluates an expression for its value; with a second text, that runs if the first fails. `evalc` returns what the code would have written to the Command Window as text. Code in text is harder to read and check than code written out, so they are best kept for what cannot be written otherwise.
syntax: The second if the first fails.

examples.title: Run, evaluated, and captured
examples.code:
eval('a = 2 + 3;')
a
x = eval('a^2')
eval('error(''boom'')', 'disp(''recovered'')')
s = evalc('disp(pi)')

pages.summary: Code run, and variables set, in the caller's or the base workspace; and the name of a variable passed in.
body: From inside a function, `evalin('caller', expr)` evaluates in the workspace that called it and `evalin('base', expr)` in the Command Window's; `assignin` sets a variable there. `inputname(k)` gives the name of the variable passed as the kth input, or '' for an expression.

examples.title: A function that reports what it was given and leaves a result

pages.summary: The name of the program file that is running; '' in the Command Window.
body: `mfilename('fullpath')` gives its folder and name without `.m`. Useful to find files kept beside a program.

examples.title: A function that names itself

pages.summary: The number of inputs and outputs a function was called with, and errors unless they are within bounds.
body: Inside a function, `nargin` and `nargout` count the inputs given and outputs asked for, so that missing inputs can take defaults and work can be skipped for outputs not wanted. `nargin(fun)` gives how many inputs a function takes (negative with `varargin`). `narginchk` and `nargoutchk` raise the language's errors when the counts are out of bounds.

examples.title: Defaults for missing inputs
examples.output:
ans =

    10    15    16

ans =

     3

Not enough input arguments.

pages.summary: An error unless a value has the classes and attributes given.
body: Classes are names (`'double'`, `'char'`, ...) or `'numeric'`, `'float'`, `'integer'`; attributes include `'scalar'`, `'vector'`, `'row'`, `'nonempty'`, `'real'`, `'finite'`, `'integer'`, `'positive'`, `'nonnegative'`, `'increasing'`, and, with a value, `'size'`, `'numel'`, `'>'`, `'<='` and the like. The message names the function and input when given.
syntax: validateattributes(x, classes, attributes, funcName, varName, argIndex)

examples.title: A check that passes and one that does not
examples.code:
validateattributes([1 2 3], {'numeric'}, {'positive', 'increasing'})
try
    validateattributes(-1, {'numeric'}, {'positive'}, 'grow', 'rate', 2)
catch e
    disp(e.message)
end
examples.output: Expected input number 2, rate, to be positive.

pages.summary: Valid variable names: tested, made from text, and made unique.
body: A name starts with a letter, holds letters, digits and underscores, is at most `namelengthmax` (63) characters and is not a keyword (`iskeyword` lists them). `matlab.lang.makeValidName` makes valid names from any text (spaces and other characters replaced, a prefix where needed); `matlab.lang.makeUniqueStrings` adds `_1`, `_2`, ... to make names unique; `genvarname` does both for one name.

examples.title: Column headings made into names
examples.code:
[isvarname('rate2') isvarname('2rate') iskeyword('end')]
names = matlab.lang.makeValidName({'Flow rate', '2nd value', 'for'})
matlab.lang.makeUniqueStrings({'x', 'x', 'y', 'x'})
genvarname('x', {'x', 'x1'})
examples.output:
ans =

  1×3 logical array

   1   0   1

names = 

  1×3 cell array

    {'FlowRate'}    {'x2ndValue'}    {'xFor'}

ans = 

  1×4 cell array

    {'x'}    {'x_1'}    {'y'}    {'x_2'}

ans =

    'x2'

pages.summary: The built-in function of a name called, even when a file of that name shadows it.
body: A program file named like a built-in function (`disp.m`) takes its place; `builtin('disp', x)` still reaches the original, as the shadowing function itself often needs to.

examples.title: A shadowing function that calls the original
examples.intro: The example writes the file and calls it at once, so the call goes through feval, which looks the name up as it runs; a call typed after the file exists finds it as well.
